'''''Lycopus europaeus''''', common names '''gypsywort, gipsywort, bugleweed, European bugleweed''' and '''water horehound''', is a [[perennial plant]] in the genus ''[[Lycopus]]'', native to Europe and Asia, and naturalized elsewhere.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date=20 February 2015}}</ref> Another species, ''[[Lycopus americanus]]'' has also been erroneously called ''L. europaeus''.<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-115903
|title=The Plant List: A Working List of All Plant Species, entry for ''Lycopus europaeus'' Walter
|access-date=20 February 2015}}</ref>
[[File:Lycopus europaeus Prague 2012 3.jpg|left|thumb|''Lycopus europeaus'', Prague]]

==Description==
Gypsywort is a rather straggly perennial plant with slender underground runners and grows to a height of about {{convert|20|to|80|cm|0|abbr=on}}. The stalkless or short-stalked leaves are in opposite pairs. The leaf blades are hairy, narrowly lanceolate-ovate, sometimes pinnately-lobed, and with large teeth on the margin. The inflorescence forms a terminal spike and is composed of dense whorls of white or pale pink flowers. The calyx has five lobes and the corolla forms a two-lipped flower about {{convert|4|mm|2|abbr=on}} long with a fused tube. The upper lip of each flower is slightly convex with a notched tip and the lower lip is three-lobed, the central lobe being the largest and bearing a red "nectar mark" to attract pollinating insects. There are two stamens, the [[gynoecium]] has two fused carpels and the fruit is a four-chambered [[schizocarp]].<ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web |url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/gipsywort |title=Gipsywort: ''Lycopus europaeus'' |publisher=NatureGate |access-date=2013-12-15}}</ref> The flowers are visited by many types of insects, and can be characterized by a generalized [[pollination syndrome]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762 | pmid = 25754608 | volume = 18| issue = 1| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

==Habitat==
Gypsywort grows primarily in [[wetland]] areas. It grows along the borders of lakes, ponds and streams as well as in canals and marshes. Its carpels float which may aid dispersal of the plant and its [[rhizome]]ous roots also allow the plant to spread.<ref name=NatureGate/>  It is in flower from June to September, and produces seeds from August to October.

==Etymology and folklore==

It is reputed to have medicinal qualities<ref name=GRIN/><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180103011538/https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/ethnoPlants/show/5305 ''Lycopus europaeus'' (Lamiaceae) - Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases]</ref><ref name="pfaf.org">[http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Lycopus+europaeus Plants for a Future Database of Edible and Medicinal Plants]</ref><ref name="Henriette's Herbal">[http://www.henriettesherbal.com/eclectic/kings/lycopus.html#rel-sp Henriette's Herbal]</ref> and has been used by various peoples as a dye, astringent, cosmetic, douche and narcotic.{{citation needed|date=November 2011}}  Several research studies have been undertaken on the properties of this plant.{{vague|date=November 2011}}<ref>[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/query.fcgi?db=PubMed&cmd=search&term=%22Lycopus+europaeus%22] List of articles from the [[National Library of Medicine]] and the [[National Institutes of Health]]</ref>

[[Rembert Dodoens]] wrote of the names of the plant in the 1578 English translation<ref name="Nievve">{{cite book|last1=Dodoens|first1=Rembert|last2=Lyte|first2=Henry|title=A Nievve Herball;…|date=1578|publisher=Mr Gerard Dewes, St Paul's Churchyard at the sign of the Swan|location=London|pages=255–258|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/30665#page/282/mode/1up|access-date=5 July 2017}}</ref> of his original book published in 1563, as the fourth among the group of horehounds “…: in [[Duchy of Brabant|Brabant]] water Andoren, and of some Egyptenaers cruyt, that is to say, the Egyptians herbe, bycause of the Rogues and runnegates which call themselves Egyptians, do colour themselves blacke with this herbe.” The Brabant original seems to suggest it was used by itinerant non-Roma who were pretending to be [[Romani people]] by darkening their skin.<ref name="Cruyde">{{cite book|last1=Dodoens|first1=Rembert|title=Crŭÿde boeck :...|date=1563|publisher=Jan vander Loe, Cammerstrate at the sign of the Scarab|location=Thantwerpen|pages=ccvv-ccvvi|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/30640#page/263/mode/1up|access-date=5 July 2017}}</ref> He also wrote that water horehound was not used in medicine.<ref name="Nievve" /> Through time it often came to be said that name gypsywort comes from the belief that Romani people would stain their skin with the juice of the plant, although Howard (1987) states that they used it to dye their linen.<ref name="pfaf.org"/><ref name="Henriette's Herbal"/><ref>Howard, Michael. ''Traditional Folk Remedies'' (Century, 1987) p.151</ref>
